name: babeld
why: A loop-avoiding distance-vector routing daemon, a door into how mesh and home routers quietly find paths to each other.

brief.what_it_is: Babel is a loop-avoiding distance-vector routing protocol for IPv6 and IPv4, implemented in the reference daemon babeld. You start babeld on each node and list the network interfaces it should take part on, for example babeld eth1. The nodes then exchange routing updates with each other and build routes to one another's addresses. It is designed for both wired networks and wireless mesh networks, and it is an IETF standard (RFC 8966).
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says Babel is based on ideas from DSDV, AODV and Cisco's EIGRP, but is designed to work well not only in wired networks but also in wireless mesh networks, and has been extended for overlay networks. The GitHub README describes it as roughly based on HSDV and AODV, with provisions for link cost estimation and redistribution of routes from other routing protocols.
brief.how_it_works: When babeld detects a wired link, it enables optimisations that make it as efficient as traditional routing protocols. When it detects a wireless link, it disables those optimisations and uses a packet-loss metric designed for 802.11 WiFi (the ETX metric), which slows convergence but keeps radio link quirks from breaking routing. Babel uses triggered updates and explicit requests for routing information, and a single update packet can carry both IPv6 and IPv4 routes.

brief.install_notes: Build from source with make, then make install as root. The README says to run git submodule init and git submodule update after cloning, and it gives no reason. Cross-compiling for OpenWRT needs a different CC and PLATFORM_DEFINES, and Mac OS X needs LDLIBS set empty. Each node needs a wireless or other interface set up, and needs unique IPv6 and/or IPv4 addresses. Some VPN or tunnel interfaces (the README names OpenVPN and Linux GRE) do not get an IPv6 link-local address automatically, so one must be added by hand or babeld fails with 'couldn't allocate requested address'. For an Internet gateway, the default route must carry an explicit protocol, such as proto static, or Babel will not redistribute it.
brief.standout: One update packet can carry both IPv6 and IPv4 routes, and the daemon switches between a wired mode with optimisations and a wireless mode with a WiFi-specific loss metric depending on link type. The protocol is an IETF standard with a family of RFCs covering authentication, DTLS, source-specific routing and Homenet, which is unusual for a small daemon.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched pages show no release date and no last-commit date. The homepage cites RFCs through RFC 9229 (May 2022) and a changelog, and it names the git repository, but I could not confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: The homepage says Babel's convergence is slow on wireless links by design, and that after heavy packet loss converging on optimal routes can take up to about 40 seconds with the default 16-second update interval. The loop-free guarantee in pure mesh networks is strong, but in prefix-based networks loops are said to vanish once an update has gone around them, not avoided outright. Some wired optimisations must be turned off manually on exotic links such as point-to-multipoint VPNs. The FRR version of Babel is described as obsolete, and Pybabel and Sbabeld are described as incomplete or not recommended. The README example commands use iwconfig and ip addr, which are older Linux tools. No licence was seen in the fetched pages.
quotes: Babel is a loop-avoiding distance-vector routing protocol for IPv6 and IPv4 with fast convergence properties.

in a pure mesh network, Babel never creates a routing loop, and in a prefix-based network, all routing loops are guaranteed to disappear as soon as one update went around a loop (there is no "counting to infinity").
